analysis.investment_thesis: Retaggio fails the Magic Formula on both axes: a trivial ROE of 0.12% implies near-zero return on capital, and a P/E of 17 delivers an earnings yield of only ~5.9%, below my 6% floor. This is neither cheap nor a good business — a textbook avoid.
key_strengths: Promoter holding is high at 60.18%, showing skin in the game
Micro-cap jewelry play in a structurally growing Indian category
Company is profitable (positive earnings) rather than loss-making
key_risks: ROE of 0.12% indicates capital is earning essentially nothing
Earnings yield ~5.9% (P/E 17) is expensive for a tiny, unproven 2022 vintage business
Jewelry manufacturing is working-capital heavy — low ROIC likely to persist
red_flags: ROE 0.12% — effectively zero return on capital
Incorporated only in 2022, no multi-year ROIC track record
Tiny ₹88.6 Cr market cap with negligible FII (1.39%) — liquidity and governance risk
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula requires a company to be both cheap and good. Retaggio is neither. On the "good" side, ROE of 0.12% is a catastrophic signal — for every ₹100 of equity, the business earns 12 paise. Even allowing for some leverage noise, ROIC cannot be meaningfully above single digits; it is far below my 20% bar. Jewelry manufacturing is inherently inventory- and working-capital-intensive (gold, WIP, receivables), which structurally caps returns on capital unless a real brand moat exists, and a 2022-incorporated micro-cap has no such moat.

On the "cheap" side, a P/E of 17 translates to an earnings yield of roughly 5.9%, below my 6% minimum and nowhere near the 12–15% I want in a Magic Formula name. Paying 17x earnings for a business earning 0.12% on equity is the opposite of the trade I look for. With only a three-year operating history, no visible competitive advantage, and metrics that fail both screens decisively, this is a clear avoid — no systematic value investor would rank this in the top decile.
